key: Thus it is that when opposing weapons are (actually) crossed, he who deplores (the situation) conquers.
s: Closing a chapter on war that begins with a saying about yielding ground, the verse speaks of armies meeting; Wang Bi, on chapter 69, takes those who grieve as sure to cherish one another, neither chasing gain nor shunning harm, and so sure to win.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 69, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

evidence.words: 抗，舉也；加，當也。哀者，必相惜而不趣利避害，故必勝。
evidence.gloss: Kang means to raise; jia means to meet. Those who grieve are sure to cherish one another and do not rush after gain or flee from harm; therefore they are sure to win.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 69, at [68]); Wang Bi’s base line 故抗兵相加，哀者勝矣 is the key verse’s line, and his comment on it carries the reading: those who grieve cherish one another, neither hasten to gain nor avoid harm, and so win. Plain sense states the war setting in plain terms (armies meeting; the chapter opens with the saying about retiring a foot rather than advancing), without softening, and leans on none of Legge’s parentheses. The limit Wang Bi sets (not chasing gain) is carried. entry-check ok, 45 words.
